newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Influx seen behind HK scorn for mainlanders.
newsitem.headline: Influx seen behind HK scorn for mainlanders.

text.p: A poll on mainland immigration shows Hong Kong people have little love for their compatriots over the border even as the clock ticks away to reunification of the British colony to China.

The survey by the Hong Kong Psychological Society released on Monday of 423 Hong Kong-born people, found 51 percent thought mainland immigrants were ignorant, rude, dirty and were introducing evils from the mainland.
Social workers said part of the problem appeared to stem from a recent influx of mainland migrants which was straining Hong Kong's resources for coping.
In 1995, the quota of mainland immigrants was increased to 150 from 105 a day, a rise of almost 43 percent.
Many of the latest wave of immigrants were competing for unskilled or semi-skilled jobs, strengthening Hong Kong stereotypes of their "hayseed" mainland cousins, they said.
More than 98 percent of Hong Kong's more than six million population is ethnic Chinese, the majority hailing from China's southern Guangdong province.

Thomas Mulvey, executive director of the Hong Kong Family Welfare Society, said there had been relatively little recognition until recently of the need to provide for new immigrants from the mainland.
Au Wai-kwong, a social worker with the Cheung Sha Wan Outreaching Team base, said mainland immigrants coming to the territory to rejoin family members often encountered problems.
Some younger mainland immigrants found the level of English they had learned in mainland schools was insufficient for English-language requirements in Hong Kong schools, Au said.

A superviser with the employment service of the Hong Kong Council of Social Services, said some mainland immigrants were well educated, but their qualifications were not recognised in the Hong Kong market.
As a result, many ended up competing for semi-skilled or unskilled work, a category in which the unemployment rate was rising, she said.
Hong Kong returns to China at midnight on June 30, ending more than 150 years of British colonial rule.
Michael DeGolyer, director of the Hong Kong 1997 Transition Project at Hong Kong's Baptist University, said a stereotype of mainland immigrants as "hayseed cousins" did exist.
"It's quite a common thing - the rural immigrant coming to Hong Kong and having to adjust to the more sophisticated ways and faster pace of life," DeGolyer said.
Mainland immigrants were often surprised by the small size of Hong Kong living quarters and by how hard people in Hong Kong had to work, DeGolyer said.
